title: Sources
text:
The data for this project comes from the World Bank’s World Development Indicators (WDI), accessed through the WDI R package.
Indicators used:

SP.DYN.LE00.IN: Life expectancy at birth, total (years)
NY.GDP.PCAP.CD: GDP per capita (current US dollars)
SH.XPD.CHEX.GD.ZS: Current health expenditure (% of GDP)

Coverage:

country-level observations
annual data from 2000 to 2023
region and income-group metadata supplied through WDI

Cleaning approach:

rename raw WDI codes into readable variables
remove observations with missing values where needed for each figure
compare countries by region and income group rather than treating all observations as identical

This setup is suitable for exploratory cross-country development analysis and can be extended later into panel regressions or more focused case studies.

title: About
text:
I am Faran Abbas, a graduate student in World Economy at Shandong University. You can view my work on GitHub or contact me at faranabbas@hotmail.com.
This project studies how life expectancy relates to income and health spending across countries using World Bank data. It is designed as a development-economics portfolio project that connects economic resources, public spending, and human well-being in a reproducible Quarto workflow.
The repository is available here.

title: Life Expectancy, Income, and Health Spending Across Countries
text:
This project explores how life expectancy differs across countries and how those differences relate to economic development and health spending.
Using the World Bank’s World Development Indicators, the analysis compares countries in the most recent year available and tracks average life expectancy across income groups over time. The goal is not to claim a causal result, but to build a clear, reproducible cross-country view of development and health outcomes.

title: Life Expectancy, Income, and Health Spending Across Countries
text:
Interpretation
This project is meant to support careful comparison rather than overclaiming. Countries with similar income levels can still have very different health outcomes, which leaves room for deeper analysis of institutions, public policy, inequality, and health-system performance.
